name: Tifal
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Boush, Al & Susan Boush. 1974. Tifal phonology (SIL ms.); Steinkraus, Walter. 1969. Tifal phonology showing vowel and tone neutralization. Kivung 2. Kivung 2(1) scan online lacks scanned; SIL search 403s.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is predictable by the following rules: Primary stress occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel. In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is closed by a consonant, primary stress occurs on the final syllable. In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is open, primary stress occurs on the initial syllable. The above rules apply to the stems of inflected words. Non-inflected words of more than three syllables in which all vowels are short are extremely rare, and stress rules have not yet been posited for them.
new_statements.citation: Steinkraus, Walter. 1969. Tifal phonology showing vowel and tone neutralization. Kivung 2(1): 57-66.
new_statements.locator: Section 7 'Stress', p. 64 (PDF p. 8); tone system in Section 6 'Tonemes', pp. 63-64
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and predictable from vowel length and syllable closure: the leftmost long-vowel syllable takes primary stress; if all vowels are short (2-3 syllable uninflected words), stress is final when the final syllable is closed and initial when it is open; in inflected verbs the rules apply to the stem (Boush & Boush 1974 and the 1994/2004 OPD phrase this as stress on the final syllable of the simple verb stem). Steinkraus analyses Tifal as also having two lexical tonemes (high/low, one per syllable, neutralized on word-initial short syllables); Boush & Boush 1974 (Balemtilabib/Lam valley dialect) found tone non-contrastive and stress 'more crucial'. The same stress rules are restated independently in Boush & Boush 1974 sec. 3.3.1 pp.25-27 and the SIL OPD (2004) p.3.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Steinkraus 1969 p.64: 'Secondary stress occurs on the second syllable with a lengthened vowel. In inflected words with more than three syllables in which all vowels are short, secondary stress occurs on the antepenult. No secondary stress occurs in words of three or less syllables in which all vowels are short.' Boush & Boush 1974 p.26: secondary stress in inflected words of four or more syllables falls on the final (suffix) syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress rules not posited for the (rare) all-short non-inflected words of more than three syllables (Steinkraus) nor for complex/compound verbs (Boush & Boush 1974 p.27).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rules stated on citation forms; separate treatment for non-inflected words vs. inflected verb stems. Steinkraus's data from Okbiilabib (Ilam valley); Boush's from Balemtilabib (Lam valley) -- Boush calls Steinkraus's a 'closely related dialect' and disagrees on the existence of contrastive tone but not on stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Steinkraus 1969 describes the Okbiilabib (Ilam river valley) variety; Boush & Boush 1974 / OPD 2004 describe the Balemtilabib (Lam river valley) variety, which Boush calls a closely related dialect of the same language (Tifal, ISO tif, tifa1245; OPD label 'Tifal (Tifalmin)'). The two agree on stress placement but differ on tone: Steinkraus posits two contrastive tonemes, Boush finds tone non-contrastive.

In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is closed by a consonant, primary stress occurs on the final syllable. sources.locator: Section 7 'Stress', p. 64 (PDF p. 8); tone system in Section 6 'Tonemes', pp. 63-64
sources.note: Sec. 7 'Stress' p.64: primary stress predictable -- on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel; in all-short-vowel 2-3 syllable non-inflected words, final syllable if closed, initial syllable if final open; same rules apply to stems of inflected words; secondary stress on the second long-vowel syllable, or on the antepenult in all-short inflected words of >3 syllables. Sec. 6 (p.63-64): two tonemes (high/low), one per syllable; tone neutralized on word-initial short-vowel syllables.

sources.citation: Boush, Al and Susan Boush. 1974. Tifal phonology. Ukarumpa: SIL unpublished ms., 43 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online
sources.note: Sec. 3.3.1 Stress pp.25-27: same three rules as Steinkraus (first long-vowel syllable; else final if closed, initial if open, in 2-3 syllable non-inflected words); inflected words: primary stress on final syllable of simple verb stem, secondary stress in inflected words of 4+ syllables on the final suffix syllable; compound/complex verb stress not posited. Fn.3 p.25: 'Thus far, tone has been found to be non-contrastive. This differs from the work done in a related dialect by Walter Steinkraus, TIFAL TONE. Stress seems to be more crucial.'

sources.citation: SIL-PNG. 2004 [data checked by Al Boush 1994]. Organised Phonology Data: Tifal (Tifalmin) language [TIF], Telefomin, Sandaun Province. 4 pp.
sources.note: p.3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Stress is predictable. It occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel, or on the final syllable of [if] all the vowels are short and the final syllable is closed. If the final syllable is open, primary stress occurs on the initial syllable. On inflected words primary stress occurs on the final syllable of a simple verb stem.' No tone mentioned.
